extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical political economy; policymakers interested in trade, taxation, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates Adam Smith's (and Quesnay/Colbertian) criteria for what counts as productive labour, how national annual produce is distributed, and which policies (trade, taxation, improvements) encourage or discourage growth. Useful for analyzing classical arguments about agriculture, manufactures, rent, and trade policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Productive vs unproductive classes (Quesnay's taxonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The population is divided into three classes: proprietors of land; cultivators (farmers and country labourers) called the 'productive class'; and artificers, manufacturers, and merchants called the 'barren or unproductive class'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quesnay's system treats only proprietors and cultivators as contributing to the annual produce; artificers/manufacturers/merchants are labelled barren because, on his view, their labour only replaces the stock which employs them. The text both explains this taxonomy and sets it up for critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for 'productive' labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Labour is productive if, over and above replacing necessary expenses (maintenance, wear of tools, seed, etc.), it yields a 'neat produce' — a surplus that constitutes rent or an addition to the annual produce of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cultivator's original and annual expenses are considered capitals that must be restored; productive labour consistently yields a net produce beyond replacing these capitals. Example: farmers reproduce a neat produce which affords rent to the landlord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground expenses as 'productive expenses' (landlord improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expenses laid out by the proprietor on land improvement (buildings, drains, inclosures) are ground or productive expenses because, after repayment with ordinary profits, they lead to reproduction of a neat produce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until repaid by advanced rent these expenses 'ought to be regarded as sacred and inviolable' (not subject to tithe or taxation), since taxing them discourages improvement and thus future tithes/taxes. Policy implication: avoid taxing or confiscating landlord-improvement capital before it is repaid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmer's original and annual expenses as capital that must be preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Original expenses (instruments, stock, seed, maintenance during first year) and annual expenses (seed, wear and tear, maintenance) are capitals employed in cultivation that must be regularly restored with reasonable profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the farmer cannot replace these expenses and earn ordinary profits, he will abandon cultivation. Therefore rent and policy should not strip away these funds; the landlord's rent should be 'no more than the neat produce which remains after paying ... all the necessary expenses'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quesnay's assertion that manufacturers/merchants are 'unproductive'
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers, manufacturers, and merchants are said to be barren/unproductive because their labour purportedly only replaces the maintenance of the stock that employs them and does not add to the value of the whole annual produce of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative example used: a lace worker who may convert a pennyworth of flax into a high-priced product but whose labour, it is argued, only replaces his subsistence and thus does not augment the annual produce in total. This is the target of Smith's critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smith's rebuttal: manufacturing and mercantile labour can add real value
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if artisans' consumption equals their production over a period, their labour 'really adds the value' to the annual produce because it fixes and realizes value in vendible commodities and increases the actually existing stock/value in the market over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith gives the six‑month example: an artificer producing ten pounds of value while consuming ten pounds increases the value of what exists (turning consumed goods into vendible products), and savings out of their revenue can increase real wealth. Anti-pattern: treating artisans as equivalent to menial servants whose services perish on delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy criterion: freedom of trade
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect freedom of trade is presented as the most effective means for a landed nation to raise the value of its surplus produce, encourage improvement and cultivation, and ultimately develop its own artificers, manufacturers, and merchants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protectionist measures (high duties, prohibitions) raise prices of foreign goods, sink the real value of agricultural surplus, raise profits in non-agricultural employments, and draw capital away from agriculture. Allowing foreign manufactures promotes competition, cheaper supply, and long‑run domestic industry development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of Colbertian/town-favouring policies (export bans, internal restraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that favor towns/manufactures over the country—such as prohibiting exportation of corn, restricting transport between provinces, and levying arbitrary taxes on cultivators—discourage agriculture and keep it below its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific anti-patterns: export bans that exclude country inhabitants from foreign markets; provincial transport restraints; degrading taxes on cultivators. These measures reduce incentives for improvement and lower national produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and balance in promoting industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising up manufactures prematurely (by protectionism) can depress a more valuable species of industry (agriculture) and thus be detrimental overall; industries should arise naturally from surplus capital created by agriculture under free trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy should avoid artificially hastening one industry at the expense of another; the 'most effectual method' is allowing freedom of trade so surplus produce and capital naturally turn to manufactures when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for augmenting national annual produce
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual produce of land and labour can be increased only by: (1) improvements in productive powers of useful labour (better ability, machinery), or (2) increases in the quantity of useful labour employed, which requires capital accumulation (savings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturing labour is especially capable of subdivision and machinery improvements; but increases in labour quantity require savings and capital, whether from artisans or landlords. Policy implication: encourage accumulation and improvements in productive methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of saving (parsimony) in augmenting wealth for non-agricultural classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificers, manufacturers, and merchants can augment the revenue and wealth of society only by saving (privations) out of their revenue; otherwise their annual reproduction of funds does not increase total wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith contrasts nations dominated by merchants/manufacturers (which grow rich chiefly through parsimony) with landed societies that can be enriched by both industry and enjoyment. Encourages policies that allow accumulation without damaging productive capitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural distribution under perfect liberty and consequences of its violation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quesnay's 'Economical Table' represents a natural distribution of the annual produce under perfect liberty; every encroachment or violation (favoring proprietors or the barren class) degrades the annual produce and causes gradual declension in real wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When institutions or policies alter this natural distribution (e.g., favor one class), the decline in wealth depends on the degree of encroachment. Policy implication: maintain impartiality and avoid institutional favoritism to preserve growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect usefulness of the 'unproductive' class via specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Though called unproductive in Quesnay's sense, merchants, artificers, and manufacturers are 'greatly useful' because they supply foreign goods and manufacturing needs cheaply and free cultivators from tasks that distract from agriculture, thereby increasing productive labour's output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports allowing liberty to the unproductive class: their competition lowers prices for proprietors/cultivators and the specialization they enable raises the productive powers of agricultural labour. Anti-pattern: restricting or oppressing this class reduces overall welfare.
